extracted.intended_audience: ship captains, pilots, and navigators entering the Port of Buenos Ayres (historical, 1824)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory and navigational rules for vessels arriving at, anchoring in, and navigating to/from the Port of Buenos Ayres (includes port police, health/quarantine procedures, anchorage dues, penalties, and detailed sailing instructions and buoy positions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard-ship arrival signalling and initial procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a vessel anchors in the outer roads the guard ship will hoist a red flag at the mizen mast as a signal to the captain of the arriving vessel to proceed to shore in his boat. On arrival the commandant will desire her to anchor astern and then hoist a yellow flag for the health boat to come and pass the visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 1–3: sequence of signals (red then yellow) and actions: captain brings papers and goes on board the guard ship; anchor astern when requested; health boat performs the visit. Article 7: after the health visit the commandant will strike the red and yellow flags. This sequence governs safe initiation of communications with shore and other vessels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on communication until health visit completes
rubrics_metrics.description: The commandant of the guard ship must not permit any communication between his crew and those of the boat, until after the health visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 4: No communication allowed until health inspection passes. If the guard-ship permits crew aboard because weather prevents the health boat, the guard-ship is considered in quarantine and must not communicate with any person until after the health visit has passed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captain to present papers and undergo health/war interrogation
rubrics_metrics.description: The captain, taking with him his papers, will go on board the guard ship and will be interrogated by the health and war visit; and if he does not answer truly, he will be tried by the laws of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 2 and 5: captains must carry papers, submit to health and war inspection, and face legal consequences for falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarantine and contagious disease signalling (yellow flag) and ships of war exception
rubrics_metrics.description: All ships in which the crew may be attacked by a contagious disorder will hoist a yellow flag and be subject to the laws of quarantine. Ships of war are an exception and are not required to conform to the stated articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 10–11: yellow flag denotes contagious disorder; guard-ship quarantine rules apply. Note the explicit exception for ships of war (Article 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when weather prevents health-boat visit
rubrics_metrics.description: If weather will not permit the health-boat to pass the visit, the commandant of the guard-ship will wait till they make signals from the shore; if weather is too boisterous and the boat cannot come on shore, the commandant may permit the crew to go on board him and then the guard-ship will be considered in a state of quarantine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 6: alternative signaling from shore; permitting crew aboard triggers quarantine status for the guard-ship until the health visit is completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchorage dues and payment schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: For foreign vessels, by the ton, four reals; for national vessels from foreign parts, two reals. The dues must be paid half on arrival and half on departure. Vessels which neither take nor receive cargo pay only half the dues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchorage Dues section: foreign vessels also pay twelve dollars on entry for the health visit and twelve more on departure for the health certificate; national vessels pay half for these. Charges for pilots are included in anchorage dues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision and placement of buoys on anchors; requirement to mark anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: It is expressly enjoined to every vessel anchored in the port to have on its anchors correspondent buoys; vessels coming in and going out not seeing the buoys run a risk of striking on the anchors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police of the Port Article 2: vessels must use anchor buoys to avoid collisions. Article 3: vessels without buoys must notify the Captain of the Port, who will send buoys with a pilot to place them. Anchor must not be raised without permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot responsibilities and duty to inform captains and report infractions
rubrics_metrics.description: At the moment of anchoring, the regular pilots will take care to inform the captains that they may provide themselves with every thing necessary for the anchorage; if the pilot discovers an infraction he will immediately inform the Captain of the Port, under penalty of being himself punished as negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police of the Port Article 4: pilots must give guidance and must report infractions; pilot negligence is punishable because it may cause 'the greatest losses and averages.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for poor anchors/cables
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in consequence of bad weather, the anchors and cables of a vessel fail to hold, and it can be proved that those same cables and anchors do not correspond with the size of the vessel, or that the cables were in bad condition, then the said vessel shall be responsible for the averages that may be occasioned thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police of the Port Article 5: vessels are accountable for losses (averages) caused by inadequate equipment/maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for not taking a pilot
rubrics_metrics.description: Every vessel from foreign parts, who moor themselves in the port, without asking for a pilot at the Captain of the Port's office, will be responsible for all the averages which may be occasioned thereby, and will have no right of claim in case they suffer damage themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police of the Port Article 6: strict liability and forfeiture of claims if a vessel fails to take a pilot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for leaving boats in way of sailing vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: Every vessel anchored, who may have its long boat or boat astern, and, seeing another vessel under sail, neglects to haul them up out of the way, not only will forfeit the right to claim in case of average, but will even be responsible for that which such negligence may occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police of the Port Article 7: keep boats clear of navigable paths; failure forfeits claim and creates liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on throwing ballast or non-floating objects overboard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is expressly forbidden to every vessel in the port to throw any thing into the water, of their ballast, or any other object that does not float, under the penalties prescribed by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police of the Port Article 8: environmental/safety prohibition with legal penalties (unspecified here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on firing salutes in inner roads
rubrics_metrics.description: It is forbidden, except at the moment of her arrival, to fire salutes, in the inner roads at least, without having first obtained permission of the Captain of the Port. The captain of a vessel who infringes upon this article will be placed at the disposal of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police of the Port Article 9: require permission; unauthorized salutes subject the captain to government custody/punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nighttime boat curfew and penalties for boats ashore
rubrics_metrics.description: Boats belonging to vessels anchored in the outer and inner roads must go on board one hour after sun-set. All boats found on shore after the evening gun, and until the morning gun has been fired, will be dismantled, and the crew punished according to the case and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police of the Port Articles 10–11: strict curfew; appliances (dismantling) and punishment applied to crews found ashore during restricted hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for destroying or tampering with government buoys
rubrics_metrics.description: To throw a kedge anchor, or hold on in any manner whatever to the said buoys, the punishment of the galleys. Those who take them away, or change their places, unless by authority of government, will be punished with all the rigour of the law, even to the penalty of death. Equally punished are those who make a fire on the said buoys, or by any other means attempt to destroy them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties section Articles 1–3: extremely severe punishments (galleys up to death) for damaging, moving, or destroying navigational buoys; Article 4 requires each captain to receive a copy of these regulations (cost included in port dues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Captain to receive printed copy of regulations (distribution and cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every captain will receive, on his arrival, a copy of these regulations; the cost of which will be included in the dues of the port. The Government approves the above regulations, orders them to be printed, and fixes the price of each copy at two reals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties section Article 4 and government approval: ensures captains are informed and ties dissemination cost to dues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sailing instructions by the North (main) channel from Outer Roads to Monte Video
rubrics_metrics.description: From three fathoms in the outer roads steer E. by S. until Point Santiago of the Ensenada of Barragan bears S.W.; off this point you will find 5½ to 6 fathoms. Proceed via Ortiz Bank when water lessens to 3–3½ fathoms, then S.E. to Point Indio, deepen to 5–5½ fathoms crossing middle channel, then when 7–9 miles from land (3¼–3½ fathoms) steer E.S.E. and coast along, keeping various courses until Monte Video is visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed stepwise compass courses and expected soundings (fathoms) at points 1–6 under 'By the North, or Main Channel.' Includes cautions about approaching Ortiz Bank (south side safer) and guidance for night/thick weather navigation using the bank as a guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sailing instructions by the South of the Chico Bank to Monte Video
rubrics_metrics.description: From 3 fathoms in the outer roads steer E. by S. until you have 6 fathoms off Ensenada; keep 5–6 miles from land after passing Ensenada, then E.S.E. to keep along the shore; use terrestrial landmarks (ombu trees, church steeples) to navigate; be aware of least water (about 17 feet) between Chico Bank and the coast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise guidance under 'By the South of the Chico Bank' with distances to landmarks, bearings for features (ombu trees, churches), and specific local depth notes such as 'when the river is low, you have generally about 17 feet' between the bank and the coast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return sailing instructions from Monte Video to Buenos Ayres (north and south of Chico Bank)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Monte Video steer S.W. thirty miles, then W.S.W. until Punta del Indio, then W. until Cape Indian bears S.S.W. 7–8 miles; when Cape Indian S.S.W., steer N.W. to make first buoys of Ortiz Bank (keep ~15 feet water), then W. keeping the two last buoys to starboard until Ensenada and Point Lara are made out. Alternate instructions provided for passing south of Chico Bank with observations to identify Punta del Indio via woods of talas and ombu trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed compass legs, distances, cautions regarding proximity to buoys and required depths (e.g., 'being cautious to have 15 feet water'), and landmark-based identification methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of terrestrial landmarks and observation techniques for position fixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous instructions identify points by distinctive trees (ombu, talas), churches (Magdalene church with two steeples), groves, and plain/copse outlines to determine bearings and to find buoys and cape positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations section and multiple route steps: use of visible trees, church steeples, groves and plain features to know positions and bearings. Example: 'Point Indio is low level land, with only one tree on it' and identification sequences using lines of ombu trees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of depth/soundings and guidance for night/poor-visibility navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed reported soundings between Monte Video and Buenos Ayres (e.g., leaving Monte Video 2½–3 fathoms; at 9 miles 5 fathoms; at 18 miles 3½ fathoms; at various legs 3–6 fathoms). Guidance: use soundings and course changes to navigate by night or when weather prevents making out marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long 'Variation of Depth' section: gives progressive soundings, where soundings increase/decrease relative to banks Ortiz and Chico, and explicit instruction: 'By the course, and the differences of soundings above-mentioned, you will be able to navigate by night, or when the weather will not permit you to make out the marks.' Also includes current directions and speeds, and tacking advice (e.g., put about when sounding gives 4 fathoms near Chico Bank).

rubrics_metrics.name: Currents and tacking guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Cape Indian to Buenos Ayres the currents flow from the E.S.E. to the W.N.W.; their rapidity is much about from 1½ to 2 miles an hour. In tacking, when the wind is contrary, a great deal of way can be made by means of the currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use current direction and speed to assist tacking and to make way when wind is unfavorable; specific tactical advice in 'Variation of Depth' and related passages (e.g., how to tack between banks and when to put about).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local bed composition and anchorage characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: In the environs of the Bank Ortiz, vessels are less subject to part from their anchors, because the bottom is mud and sand. Between the Banks Chico and Ortiz, the anchorage is good, and the anchors hold tolerably well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational guidance for anchoring decisions: prefer areas with mud/sand bottoms (Ortiz) for better holding; beware rocky parts of Chico Bank where anchors will not hold (e.g. parts with only 1½ fathom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Positions, colors, and bearings of the ten buoys (Chico, Ortiz, Santiago, Lara)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed positions and characteristics: Bank Chico has four red buoys with specific sequence (1st at S.E. extremity on 3 fathoms, bearings to Magdalene church, distances between buoys and fathoms noted); Bank Ortiz has four black buoys with positions and bearings; Ensenada de Barragan (Santiago and Lara) have two black buoys with specified bearings and bottoms (3 and 2 fathoms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'POSITIONS of the TEN BUOYS' section: each buoy numbered with relative position (compass bearings, distances in miles, and bottom depth in fathoms) and guidance that the two buoys at Santiago and Lara 'are placed to warn Navigators to pass to the Northward.' Includes observations on non-parallelism of Chico Bank and bay-like formations and their implications for navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific hazard warnings and safe-distance rules around banks and buoys
rubrics_metrics.description: Bank Chico is full of pointed rocks particularly near the second buoy (places with only 1½ fathom); when sounding line does not give more than 4 fathoms near Bank Chico you must put about ship. There is a ridge of rocks extending more than 5 miles from land near Magdalene—do not anchor nearer than 6 or 7 miles from the shore in that stretch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations sections and 'In tacking' notes: concrete thresholds for action based on sounding (e.g., 4 fathoms, 3 fathoms, 1½ fathom) and geographic markers where anchoring or approaching is unsafe. Use buoys and soundings to avoid rocky shoals.
